title: How Resilient Is Your Team?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that leaders should ask how resilient the team is, not just how resilient each member is. Individual resilience is a byproduct of prevailing in adversity, and resilient members are valuable. But the author claims that the team's resilience, not the sum of its individuals, best predicts performance under trying conditions. Resilient teams confront adversity as a unit and do not let one member's fears color the group's commitment. Trust and mutual commitment drive this, and leaders foster it by making members more accountable to each other than to the leader. That means sharing leadership responsibilities and expecting members to comfort, encourage, challenge and confront one another without waiting for the leader.
points: Resilience comes from prevailing in difficulty, so untested people and teams have not yet shown it.
Team resilience, not individual resilience, best predicts performance under pressure.
Trust and commitment to one another are what make a team resilient.
Leaders build resilience by sharing leadership and making members accountable to each other rather than to the leader.
quotes: Resilience is born under strife. As people stare adversity in the face, they either figure out a way to overcome it or wilt to the threats and pressures it creates. Those lucky enough not to experience any real adversity remain untested. For the rest of us, resilience is a byproduct of prevailing in difficult situations.

Knowing that a particular team member is highly resilient gives leaders insight into how they might handle a roadblock or a disappointment. Team members with the grit and perseverance to overcome obstacles and fight through adversity are worth their weight in gold.

But when examining the positive qualities of a team, the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. The more interesting question to ask is how resilient the team is. It is the resilience of the team, not the collective individuals, that will best predict superior performance under trying conditions.

Great teams face adversity together. That’s what makes them resilient. They hold hands and confront the challenge as a unit, not allowing the fears of any one team member to color their commitment to overcome the obstacle.

Teams that have a high degree of trust and commitment to each other are resilient teams. Leaders who foster a climate where team members feel more accountable to each other, rather than to the leader, promote more resilience.
When a team member needs to be comforted, encouraged, challenged or confronted, great teams don’t wait for the leader to interject and address the issue. They are empowered and expected to do it.
